title: The Rumour Economy
author: Andrea Chiarelli
summary: Chiarelli and three collaborators examine what happens to organisational culture when the ground is moving, as in mergers, reorganisations and leadership transitions. They offer four insights: an unofficial organisation of gatekeepers and informal power takes over when the formal one is mistrusted; culture works as an information environment before it is a set of values; culture is an identity economy in which people protect status and belonging; and uncertainty produces hidden rules that favour self-protection over excellence. Drawing on shadow-system theory, sensemaking and merger research, the essay argues that rumour fills any gap leaders leave. The practical conclusion is that leaders should treat information as a design problem, make decisions legible and protect people who surface risks early. It sits in Leadership because it is about organisational culture and change leadership.
points: Culture does not follow the org chart; the informal network of gatekeepers, translators and trusted few decides who is heard when formal structure is in flux.
Disagreement turns personal when the information environment is polluted, so leaders shape culture more by the quality of information than by slogans.
Mergers expose an identity economy in which a colleague's success can look like a forecast of one's own redundancy, so collaboration starts to feel risky.
Under uncertainty people optimise for survival, and bad habits persist because the conditions for accountability deteriorate.
The remedy is practical: name what is known and unknown, make decisions and owners legible, and protect those who raise legitimate risks early.
quotes: We talk about organisational culture as if it were a mood: upbeat or toxic, strong or weak, aligned or fragmented. In practice, culture is a web of shared assumptions about what is safe to say, how decisions really get made, what “good” looks like, who counts and what happens when you challenge the room. Most of those rules are not written down. You learn them by watching what happens to people.

You can redraw reporting lines in a day, but you cannot rewire credibility and influence at the same speed. So, in practice, culture doesn’t follow the org chart; it’s the org chart that tries to catch up with culture.

If leaders want to shape culture, they should think less about slogans and more about the quality of the information environment that people experience. Predictability and clarity lower the social cost of participation; vague reassurance raises it, by forcing individuals to do their own private risk calculations.
The old signals of identity, status and competence can be devalued without warning. People who were central become peripheral. People who were unknown in an organisation suddenly become essential.

When the environment feels safe, cooperation is rational. When the environment feels volatile, self-protection becomes rational instead. People gravitate towards the herd: they try to avoid being isolated and invest in alliances that reduce perceived risk.

Pressure doesn’t create a new culture from scratch. It accelerates whatever is already latent, and it does so through mechanisms that are easy to miss if you only look at values statements and engagement surveys.

When people can see that telling the truth is safe, the unofficial organisation starts rewarding different behaviour. Translators help with clarity rather than politics. Gatekeepers become conduits rather than obstacles. The system learns that raising problems is part of continuous improvement rather than a career hazard.
